extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of classical mechanics/statics (advanced undergraduates, graduate students, historians of science)
extracted.subtask_description: A textbook-style exposition and historical discussion of the fundamental principles of statics: Stevinus' inclined plane and funicular constructions, the parallelogram (composition) of forces, Varignon's deductions, Bernoulli's treatment and critique, experimental verification, and the principle of virtual velocities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stevinus' principle for the inclined plane
rubrics_metrics.description: If the form of the machine's motion is preserved, the proportion between force and load remains the same (Stevinus applies his pulley reasoning to the inclined plane).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stevinus conceives the load Q attached to a properly weighted string passing over a pulley normal to the inclined plane (a 'funicular' machine). By preserving the form of motion one can replace a load on an inclined plane by an equivalent string/pulley arrangement and thereby ascertain portions of weight that tend to move downwards. Example construction: draw a vertical, cut off portion ab corresponding to Q, draw perpendiculars to obtain P/Q = AC/AB = ac/ab so ac represents the string tension. Stevinus used this to extend pulley results to planes and other machines; the method is constructive and geometric rather than algebraic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Funicular machine / funicular polygon construction
rubrics_metrics.description: A method of replacing general arrangements of loads on planes by strings and pulleys (funicular machines) and of determining tensions by geometric construction (funicular polygon).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Replace loads by appropriately weighted strings passing over pulleys normal to planes; draw vertical lines and perpendiculars to obtain ratios of tensions (e.g., ac for tension of string aA). For ramifying systems of strings, produce lines and cut off portions, draw parallels (Fig. 23–25) — tensions of strings are proportional to constructed segments. This yields tensions for special cases (e.g., rectangular components) and for funicular polygons by geometric construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of the parallelogram of forces (composition of forces)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a body is acted on by two forces whose directions coincide with lines AB and AC and whose magnitudes are proportional to AB and AC, the two forces produce the same effect as a single force acting in the direction of the diagonal AD of the parallelogram ABCD and proportional to that diagonal (components and resultant).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Components are AB and AC; resultant is AD. Conversely a single force may be replaced by two or several other forces. Application examples: strings loaded exactly proportional to AB and AC produce the same effect as a single weight proportional to AD. This principle underlies composition and resolution of forces in statics and is used to treat machines and equilibrium problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Varignon's parallelogram/moments theorem and deduction from dynamics
rubrics_metrics.description: Varignon's geometrical theorem: for a parallelogram with sides p and q and diagonal r, from any point m draw perpendiculars u, v, w to these lines; then p·u + q·v = r·w. Using the observation that forces are proportional to motions produced in equal time intervals, Varignon advances from composition of motions to composition of forces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret pu, qv, rw as moments of the concurrent forces with respect to point m. If m lies in the direction of the resultant the two moments pu and qv are equal. Varignon uses this to deduce the law of the lever, to show equilibrium conditions (resultant perpendicular to plane for an inclined plane), and to found statics on dynamical considerations (treating equilibrium as special case of dynamics).

rubrics_metrics.name: Derivation of the law of the lever from the parallelogram principle
rubrics_metrics.description: If two coplanar forces are displaced along their lines of action to intersect at a point M and their resultant passes through a fixed axis point O, equilibrium obtains; from perpendiculars u and v dropped from O one has p·u = q·v, yielding the lever law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Move forces along their lines of action to a common intersection and construct parallelogram; if resultant's direction passes through the axis (immovable point) no motion occurs. Using perpendicular distances from axis to lines of action yields the lever law as a special case of Varignon's theorem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Special statical verifications of the parallelogram principle
rubrics_metrics.description: In special and symmetric cases the parallelogram principle admits easy verification (e.g., any number of equal forces acting at a point with equal angular spacing are in equilibrium; three equal forces at 120° balance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: three equal forces OA, OB, OC at 120°—each two hold the third in equilibrium; concurrent forces in same/opposite directions produce simple sum/difference results as limiting cases of the general principle. These cases are useful sanity-checks and introductory demonstrations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bernoulli's geometrical deduction of the parallelogram and critique
rubrics_metrics.description: Bernoulli attempted a purely geometrical demonstration: e.g., for two equal perpendicular forces the resultant lies along the angle bisector and its magnitude is the diagonal of the square on the side p; he generalized to unequal rectangular components and obtained r^2 = p^2 + q^2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bernoulli's method simulates ignorance of the proposition and derives it from few assumptions, but the author critiques that Bernoulli tacitly uses experiential assumptions (directional effects, replaceability of forces) and may obscure the necessary empirical premises. Bernoulli's work reveals how few experiences suffice but warns to keep all assumptions explicit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assumptions about forces: magnitude and direction as sole decisive factors and replaceability by weights
rubrics_metrics.description: Statics treats force as a pull or pressure that can be replaced by the pull/pressure of a weight; the decisive factors are magnitude and direction (measurable by weights and known by the direction of motion or a stretched cord).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This tacit assumption underlies many deductions: that a force's effect in any direction is measured by its projection (p cos a); that several forces acting at a point are replaceable by a single force; and that forces can be compared/represented by weights. The text emphasises these are empirical observations and must not be hidden when giving deductions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of projection (force effect measured by projection: p·cos a)
rubrics_metrics.description: The effect of a force in any given direction can be measured by its projection on that direction; equivalently, a force inclined by angle a has an effect equivalent to p·cos a in that direction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The principle of projection is mathematically equivalent to the parallelogram of forces and is often a more direct experiential route to it. Bernoulli and others tacitly assume this; Poisson's deductions show that if any other function of angle were substituted, consistency forces the cosine form. The projection principle is used in analytic derivations and assertions of replaceability.

rubrics_metrics.name: General principle of equivalence of several forces to a single force
rubrics_metrics.description: The empirical observation that any system of forces acting at a point is replaceable, in every respect and in every direction, by a single determinate force (magnitude and direction).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mathematically equivalent to the parallelogram/projection principle but a stronger empirical claim; the text warns that deducing the parallelogram from this stronger premise is possible but less economical. The assumption requires wide experience to justify and is nontrivial (forces independence assumption enters here).

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental verification apparatus (Cauchy's test of the parallelogram)
rubrics_metrics.description: Cauchy's apparatus: centre of a horizontal divided circle with three threads tied at a point and passed over grooved wheels fixed around the circumference, loaded by weights. Proper placement and weights demonstrate equilibrium predicted by the parallelogram principle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example experiments: three equal weights at 0°, 120°, 240° yield the knot just above the centre showing equilibrium; for arbitrary p and q construct the parallelogram, add an equal and opposite force — place wheels at the constructed angles and load strings with p, q, r; the knotted point will be at the circle centre. This provides direct laboratory confirmation of the principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of virtual velocities (virtual displacements)
rubrics_metrics.description: The principle of virtual velocities (vitesse virtuelle): the truth that equilibrium can be investigated by considering possible (virtual) displacements; first remarked by Stevinus in pulley investigations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used for analysis of equilibrium of pulleys and combinations; the term 'virtual' indicates existing in effect but not actually. The principle allows reasoning about equilibrium by imagining infinitesimal permissible displacements and equating virtual work/velocity considerations; the text introduces historical attribution and usage (Bernoulli coined 'vitesse virtuelle').

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction methods for composition/resolution of multiple forces (ramifying strings)
rubrics_metrics.description: Geometric procedures to determine tensions in systems of several strings (e.g., three strings at arbitrary angles, ramifying systems) by extending, cutting off segments, and drawing parallels so tensions are proportional to constructed segments (Stevinus' constructions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure examples: extend AB to X and cut off AE, draw EF // AD and EG // AC; tensions of AB, AC, AD proportional to AE, AF, AG respectively. For ramifying systems start from a given vertical tension and propagate via similar constructions. Funicular polygon constructions (Fig. 25) give tensions of systems in equilibrium.
